7 ways to make your business visible in the GTA

Most local customers find a business in one of two ways: they search for it, or they see it. Here are seven practical ways to be seen more often — and how to make each one count.

By the Satin Graphic teamUpdated October 10, 2026

Start with the basics: be findable and consistent

Before spending on signage or print, make sure people who see your name can find you. Claim and complete your Google Business Profile: correct category, hours, phone, website, service area and real photos of your work, your team and your storefront or vehicles. Use exactly the same business name, address and phone number on your website, your profile, your vehicles and your printed materials. Consistency helps customers trust what they see, and it avoids the frustration of a wrong number printed on a van.

Then pick one visual identity — logo, two or three brand colours, one or two fonts — and use it everywhere. Each of the seven channels below works better when people recognise it as the same company.

1. Storefront and window graphics

If you have a storefront, the glass is your most valuable advertising space. Someone walking or driving past decides in seconds whether you’re open, what you sell and whether it’s for them.

  • Hours, logo and phone on the door — single-colour window decals are inexpensive and easy to update.
  • A large, readable message for drivers — perforated vinyl carries a full-colour image outside while you still see out from inside.
  • Privacy with branding — frosted vinyl with a cut-out logo works well for clinics and offices.

Most plazas require landlord approval and sometimes a municipal sign permit for exterior signage, so check before you order. Our storefront window graphics guide compares the options in detail.

2. Vehicle lettering and wraps

For trades, home services, delivery and mobile businesses, the vehicle is often the biggest sign the business owns — and it is parked in customers’ driveways, in busy plazas and on the 400-series highways every day. Even simple vehicle lettering with your name, service and phone number turns a work van into a moving business card; a commercial wrap makes it unmistakable.

Keep the message short: who you are, what you do, and one way to contact you. A phone number or web address should be readable from the next lane. If you’re unsure how much coverage you need, see our guide to lettering vs partial vs full wraps, and our fleet wrap ROI guide shows how to work out whether it pays for itself.

3. Sidewalk signs and flags

For street-front shops, cafés and service counters, a sidewalk sign catches people at walking pace. An A-frame sign with interchangeable faces lets you change the offer weekly. Feather and teardrop flags add height and movement for plazas, grand openings and car lots where your sign is set back from the road.

Many municipalities, including Toronto, regulate signs placed on the public sidewalk or boulevard, and plazas often have their own rules — check before you put anything out in front of the property line.

4. Yard signs and lawn signs

If you work at customers’ homes — landscaping, roofing, renovation, painting, pools, real estate — a sign on the lawn during and after the job is seen by the neighbours most likely to need the same service. Ask the homeowner’s permission, keep the sign simple (logo, service, phone or website) and collect it when the job ends. Corrugated plastic yard signs with H-stakes are reusable; poly bag lawn signs are the budget option for large quantities. Our yard sign guide covers sizes, prices and local rules.

5. Printed pieces that stay in people’s hands

Print still works when it reaches the right people at the right moment.

  • Business cards for every conversation — see our business card design rules.
  • Door hangers for the streets around a job you’re already working on.
  • Postcards for direct mail. Canada Post’s neighbourhood mail service can deliver unaddressed mail to chosen routes; check its current options and rates.
  • Flyers for counters, community boards and events.

Give every printed piece a single offer and a way to track it — a dedicated landing page, a promo code or a QR code — so you know what worked.

6. Banners and displays for events

Trade shows, community festivals, farmers’ markets and open houses put you in front of hundreds of local people in a day. A roll-up banner sets up in a minute and makes even a folding table look professional; a vinyl banner with grommets works on fences, tents and storefronts for grand openings. See our roll-up banner and trade show guide for sizes and design tips.

7. Branded apparel

Uniforms do two jobs: customers know who just knocked on the door, and your team advertises the business at the coffee shop, the hardware store and the job site. Branded T-shirts, hoodies, hats and workwear are inexpensive per piece and there’s no minimum order at our shop. Our custom apparel printing guide explains which decoration method suits which garment.

Measure what works

Ask every new customer how they heard about you and write it down. Use a different phone number, landing page or promo code on different channels where you can. Within a few months you’ll know which of the seven is worth doubling down on — and which to drop. If you’d like help putting a plan together, our team can design and produce everything from the van to the business cards under one roof, and our social media and website design services cover the online side.

Questions

What is the cheapest way to advertise a local business?
A complete Google Business Profile costs nothing. After that, the lowest-cost physical options are usually window decals, vehicle lettering, yard signs and business cards — each is a one-time cost that keeps working.
Do I need a permit for a storefront sign in Vaughan or Toronto?
Exterior signs often need landlord approval and may need a municipal sign permit; rules differ between municipalities and sign types. Check with your landlord and the city before installing. We can supply drawings for an application.
Is vehicle lettering worth it for a small business?
For most service businesses, yes: it costs about 22% of a full wrap and puts your name in front of people every day the vehicle is on the road or parked at a job.
How do I know which advertising is working?
Ask every new customer how they found you, and use separate phone numbers, landing pages or promo codes for different channels where you can.
